paper.title: DSSSB TGT Mathematics 2021 (2 September, shift 3)
paper.source: DSSSB TGT Mathematics (Male), computer-based test of 2 September 2021, shift 3: the mathematics section (questions 101 to 190) of the board's question-paper preview, with the board's answer key
paper.note: The mathematics section of the paper; the whole paper had 200 questions in 120 minutes.

en.q: What is domain of definition of exponential function?
en.explanation: $e^x$ (or $a^x$ with $a>0$) is defined for every real $x$, so its domain is $\mathbb{R}$; its range is $(0,\infty)$.
notes: Too small: $e^x$ is defined between the integers too.
Too small: negative and fractional $x$ are allowed.
Too small: irrational exponents such as $e^{\sqrt2}$ are defined too.
facts: Exponential function: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $(0,\infty)$.

en.q: In what range does $\sec(x)$ become invertible?
en.explanation: $|\sec x|=1/|\cos x|\ge1$, so the range of $\sec x$ is $\mathbb{R}-(-1,1)$. Restricted to $[0,\pi]-\{\pi/2\}$ it is one-one onto this set, so $\sec^{-1}x$ is defined exactly for $x\in\mathbb{R}-(-1,1)$.
notes: Correct: the range of sec, i.e. the domain of $\sec^{-1}$.
Values such as $0.5$ must still be excluded.
Not related to the values of sec.
facts: Domain of $\sec^{-1}x$ and $\csc^{-1}x$: $|x|\ge1$, i.e. $\mathbb{R}-(-1,1)$.

en.q: Asymptotes are the tangents to the curve at which point?
en.explanation: An asymptote is a straight line whose distance from a point of the curve tends to $0$ as the point moves off to infinity along the curve. It is the limiting position of the tangent, i.e. the tangent at infinity.
notes: Correct: an asymptote touches the curve at infinity.
A tangent at a finite point is an ordinary tangent.
Touching at finite points does not make a line an asymptote.
Touching at finite points does not make a line an asymptote.
facts: An asymptote is a tangent to the curve at infinity.

en.q: The curve given by $xy=15$ is symmetrical about what?
en.explanation: Interchanging $x$ and $y$ leaves $xy=15$ unchanged, so the curve is symmetric about the line $y=x$. Replacing $(x,y)$ by $(-x,-y)$ also leaves it unchanged, so it is symmetric about the origin too. Changing only the sign of $y$ (or of $x$) gives $xy=-15$: no symmetry about either axis. So (d) is also correct; the board's key is (c).
notes: Correct (key): swapping $x$ and $y$ leaves the equation unchanged.
Also true: $(-x)(-y)=xy$; the branches lie in opposite quadrants.
facts: Equation unchanged when $x\leftrightarrow y$: symmetric about $y=x$; unchanged when $(x,y)\to(-x,-y)$: symmetric about the origin.

en.q: What is the volume of curve between the ordinate 0 to 4 around the curve $x=y$?
en.explanation:
The paper's wording is garbled; it is read as: the region under the line $y=x$ between the ordinates $x=0$ and $x=4$ is revolved about the $x$-axis. It sweeps out a cone of radius 4 and height 4.
$$V=\pi\int_0^4x^2\,dx=\frac{64\pi}{3}\approx21.33\pi$$
Check: $\tfrac13\pi r^2h=\tfrac13\pi\cdot16\cdot4$.
notes: $64/3$ rounded down; the exact value is $21\tfrac13\pi$.
path: 7.6 Volumes and surfaces of solids of revolution — formulas
facts: Volume about the $x$-axis: $V=\pi\int_a^by^2\,dx$.

en.q: What is the curved surface area of cone in general form?
en.explanation: Cut the curved surface along a slant line and open it out: it is a sector of radius $l$ and arc length $2\pi r$, of area $\tfrac12\cdot2\pi r\cdot l=\pi rl$, where $l=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$ is the slant height.
notes: That is the total surface area (it adds the base $\pi r^2$).
Uses the height instead of the slant height.
Not even an area (it has the dimension of a volume).
facts: Cone: CSA $=\pi rl$, TSA $=\pi r(r+l)$, $l=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$.

en.q: If the inner product between the vectors vanishes then what will be the angle between them?
en.explanation: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta$. For non-zero vectors, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$ gives $\cos\theta=0$, so $\theta=90^\circ$: the vectors are perpendicular.
notes: At $0^\circ$ the dot product is $|\vec a||\vec b|$, its largest value.
facts: Non-zero vectors: $\vec a\perp\vec b\iff\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$.

en.q: Find the gradient of the scalar field if $f(x,y)=x+y$ at $(1,2)$?
en.explanation: $\nabla f=f_x\,\hat i+f_y\,\hat j=1\,\hat i+1\,\hat j$, the same at every point, so at $(1,2)$ it is $\hat i+\hat j$.
notes: Puts the coordinates of the point in place of the partial derivatives.
Puts the coordinates of the point in place of the partial derivatives.
facts: $\nabla f=(f_x,f_y,f_z)$; a linear $f$ has a constant gradient.

en.q: If $\vec A=3\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$; $\vec B=5\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$; $\vec C=\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ then find the volume of parallelopiped if $\vec A,\vec B,\vec C$ are sides of parallelopiped respectively?
notes: Zero would mean the three vectors are coplanar.
facts: Volume of the parallelepiped on $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$: $|[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]|$.

en.q: Find the middle term of A.P. if it is given that sum of three numbers in A.P. is 15?
en.explanation: Take the numbers as $a-d,\ a,\ a+d$. Their sum is $3a=15$, so the middle term is $a=5$, whatever $d$ is.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: For three numbers in AP take $a-d,a,a+d$: the middle term is the sum divided by 3.

en.q: A polynomial with real coefficients of $n$ degree has ________ roots?
en.explanation: By the fundamental theorem of algebra a polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ roots in $\mathbb{C}$, counted with multiplicity. With real coefficients the non-real roots come in conjugate pairs, so some roots may be real and some imaginary.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: Degree $n$ ⇒ exactly $n$ complex roots (with multiplicity); non-real roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs.

en.q: If discriminant $D>0$ then what can you say about nature of roots?
en.explanation: The roots of $ax^2+bx+c=0$ are $\frac{-b\pm\sqrt D}{2a}$. If $D>0$, $\sqrt D$ is real and non-zero, so the two roots are real and unequal.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $D>0$: real and distinct; $D=0$: real and equal; $D<0$: non-real conjugates.

en.q: Find total number of asymmetric relations on a set $A=\{e,f,g\}$?
en.explanation: An asymmetric relation contains no pair $(a,a)$, and for each of the $\binom32=3$ pairs of distinct elements $\{a,b\}$ it contains $(a,b)$, or $(b,a)$, or neither: 3 choices. So the number is $3^3=27$; in general $3^{n(n-1)/2}$.
notes: $2^6$ counts the irreflexive relations; asymmetry is ignored.
facts: On an $n$-element set: asymmetric relations $3^{n(n-1)/2}$; antisymmetric $2^n\,3^{n(n-1)/2}$; irreflexive $2^{n^2-n}$.

en.q: $2587322568103$ is a number which is divisible by which number?
en.explanation: It is odd, so not divisible by 2. Its digit sum is 52, not a multiple of 9. Its alternating digit sum is $-2$, not a multiple of 11. For 7, split into 3-digit groups from the right, $2|587|322|568|103$, and alternate signs: $103-568+322-587+2=-728=-7\times104$. So it is divisible by 7.
notes: The digit sum 52 is not a multiple of 9.
facts: Test for 7, 11 and 13 at once: alternating sum of 3-digit groups from the right (because $1001=7\cdot11\cdot13$).

en.q: Euler function tends to infinity if which condition follows?
en.explanation: Euler's function $\phi(n)$ counts the $k$, $1\le k\le n$, coprime to $n$. It satisfies $\phi(n)\ge\sqrt{n/2}$, so $\phi(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ (e.g. $\phi(p)=p-1$ for primes). It is defined only for positive integers, so the other options make no sense.
notes: $\phi$ is defined only on positive integers.
On a bounded set of integers $\phi$ stays bounded.
facts: $\phi(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$; indeed $\phi(n)\ge\sqrt{n/2}$.

en.q: How many subsets of set $A$ occurs if $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$?
en.explanation: Each element is either in a subset or not, so a set of $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets: $2^4=16$.
notes: That is the number of elements.

en.q: For any matrix to be in row reduced form which of the following conditions is not satisfied?
options: Any row if has zero is at the bottom
Each leading one is to the right of one preceding row
zero row is at the top of the matrix
en.explanation: Row echelon (reduced) form: zero rows lie at the bottom; the leading entry of each non-zero row is 1; each leading 1 lies to the right of the leading 1 of the row above (and in reduced form is the only non-zero entry of its column). Zero rows at the top break the first rule.
notes: Correct: zero rows go to the bottom, not the top.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: Echelon form: zero rows at the bottom, leading 1s stepping to the right.

en.q: What will be the rank of every non singular matrix of order $n$?
en.explanation: A non-singular $n\times n$ matrix has $|A|\ne0$, a non-zero minor of order $n$, and there are no minors of larger order. So its rank is $n$.
notes: The rank can never exceed the order.
The rank can never exceed the order.
The rank can never exceed the order.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: $A_{n\times n}$ is non-singular $\iff\rho(A)=n$.

en.q: The rank of a matrix in echelon form is equal to:
options: Number of non zero rows of the matrix
number of zero rows of the matrix
en.explanation: In echelon form the non-zero rows are linearly independent (their leading entries lie in different columns) and zero rows add nothing, so the rank equals the number of non-zero rows.
notes: Zero rows contribute nothing to the rank.
That belongs to a system of equations, not to the matrix.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: Rank = number of non-zero rows of an echelon form.

en.q: What is the limit point of the sequence $\langle f\rangle=1$?
en.explanation: The paper prints '<f>= 1' (the subscript is lost); it is read as the constant sequence $f_n=1$, i.e. $1,1,1,\dots$. Every neighbourhood of $1$ contains $f_n$ for all $n$, and no other point has this property. So its only limit point is $1$; the sequence also converges to 1.
facts: A constant sequence $\langle c\rangle$ has the single limit point $c$ (though its range $\{c\}$, as a set, has none).

en.q: The greatest limit point of a bounded sequence is called?
en.explanation: A bounded sequence has a greatest and a least limit point (Bolzano–Weierstrass). The greatest is the limit superior $\limsup f_n$ (upper limit); the least is $\liminf f_n$.
notes: That is the least limit point.
A largest term need not be a limit point.
A smallest term need not be a limit point.
facts: $\limsup$ = greatest limit point, $\liminf$ = least; a bounded sequence converges iff they are equal.

en.q: Any non-empty set of $\mathbb{R}$ which is bounded above has a ________?
en.explanation: This is the completeness (least upper bound) axiom of $\mathbb{R}$: a non-empty subset bounded above has a supremum (l.u.b.) in $\mathbb{R}$. It need not have a g.l.b.: $(-\infty,0)$ is bounded above but not below.
notes: A g.l.b. needs the set to be bounded below.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Completeness: non-empty and bounded above ⇒ $\sup$ exists in $\mathbb{R}$.

en.q: If cardinality of a set $A$ is 6 and that of set $B$ is 7 then find the cardinality of $A\Delta B$?
en.explanation: $|A\Delta B|=|A|+|B|-2|A\cap B|=13-2|A\cap B|$. Since $|A\cap B|$ can be anything from 0 to 6, $|A\Delta B|$ can be 13, 11, 9, 7, 5, 3 or 1: it cannot be determined from the data.
facts: $|A\Delta B|=|A|+|B|-2|A\cap B|$.

en.q: Every bounded sequence with a unique limit point is ________?
en.explanation: For a bounded sequence $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ are its greatest and least limit points. If there is only one limit point $l$, then $\limsup=\liminf=l$, so the sequence converges to $l$.
notes: A bounded sequence cannot diverge to $\pm\infty$.
A bounded oscillating sequence has at least two limit points.
facts: Bounded with exactly one limit point ⇔ convergent.

en.q: Pick the wrong statement?
options: Any real Cauchy sequence is convergent
In real every bounded monotonic sequence is divergent
en.explanation: (a), (b) and (c) are standard theorems; (c) is Cauchy's general principle of convergence in $\mathbb{R}$. (d) is false: a bounded monotonic real sequence converges, to its supremum if increasing and to its infimum if decreasing.
notes: Correct (the wrong statement): bounded monotonic sequences converge.
facts: Monotone convergence theorem: bounded and monotonic ⇒ convergent.

en.q: Let $\langle f_n\rangle$ be a sequence of bounded functions and the sequence is uniformly convergent to some function, say $g$; then ________.
en.explanation: The paper prints 'series given by f is uniformly continous to some function'; it is read as: the sequence $\langle f_n\rangle$ converges uniformly to $g$. Choose $N$ with $|f_N(x)-g(x)|<1$ for all $x$ (uniform convergence). If $|f_N(x)|\le M$, then $|g(x)|\le|f_N(x)|+1\le M+1$ for all $x$. So the uniform limit of bounded functions is bounded.
notes: Uniform closeness to a bounded $f_N$ rules this out.
facts: A uniform limit of bounded functions is bounded; of continuous functions, continuous.

en.q: What condition is satisfied if sequence of functions $f$ is said to be uniformly bounded?
options: $|f(x)|\le M$ for some constant $M$ and for all values of $x$
en.explanation: A sequence $\langle f_n\rangle$ is uniformly bounded when one constant $M$ works for every $n$ and every $x$: $|f_n(x)|\le M$. (Pointwise bounded would let $M$ depend on $x$.)
notes: Equality would force $|f|$ to be constant.
That is about convergence, not boundedness.
That is about convergence, not boundedness.
facts: Uniformly bounded: one $M$ with $|f_n(x)|\le M$ for all $n$ and all $x$.

en.q: The solution of the curve given $y=f(x)$, where $y$ is the function of $x$, also $x$ and $y$ are real numbers and is termed as what?
en.explanation: The graph of a solution $y=f(x)$ of a differential equation is called a solution curve (integral curve). The general solution gives a one-parameter family of such curves.
notes: A solution need not be a polynomial.
facts: Graph of a particular solution of a differential equation = solution (integral) curve.

en.q: How many singular solutions occur for $n$th order ordinary linear differential equation?
en.explanation: Every solution of a linear equation $y^{(n)}+p_1y^{(n-1)}+\dots+p_ny=q$ is contained in its general solution $y=c_1y_1+\dots+c_ny_n+y_p$. A singular solution is one not obtainable from the general solution, so a linear equation has none; they occur in non-linear equations such as Clairaut's.
notes: Correct: the general solution contains every solution.
facts: Linear ODEs have no singular solutions; Clairaut's equation $y=px+f(p)$ does.

en.q: When the per capita rate of increase $(r)$ takes the same positive value regardless of the population size, then we get which growth?
en.explanation: A constant per-capita rate means $\frac1N\frac{dN}{dt}=r$, i.e. $\frac{dN}{dt}=rN$, whose solution is $N=N_0e^{rt}$: exponential growth. In logistic growth the per-capita rate $r(1-N/K)$ falls as $N$ grows.
notes: Logistic: the per-capita rate decreases as $N$ grows.
Only one model has a constant rate.
facts: $dN/dt=rN\Rightarrow N=N_0e^{rt}$ (J-shaped); logistic $dN/dt=rN(1-N/K)$ is S-shaped.

en.q: The curve obtained in exponential growth is of which type?
en.explanation: $N=N_0e^{rt}$ rises slowly at first and then ever more steeply, without levelling off: a J-shaped curve. The logistic curve levels off at the carrying capacity $K$ and is S-shaped (sigmoid).
facts: Exponential growth: J-curve; logistic growth: S-curve.

en.q: Change in number of individuals in population over time is called?
en.explanation: The change in population size per unit time, $\frac{dN}{dt}$ (or $\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta t}$), is the population growth rate. Mortality (deaths) and immigration (arrivals) are only parts of that change.
facts: Growth rate $dN/dt$ = (births + immigrants) − (deaths + emigrants) per unit time.

en.q: Which of the following is used in mathematical modelling in Boolean algebra?
en.explanation: Constructive solid geometry builds complicated solids from simple ones (cubes, cylinders, spheres) by the Boolean operations union, intersection and difference: Boolean algebra of sets used to model shapes.
notes: Works with complex numbers, not Boolean operations.
facts: CSG: solids combined by union ($\cup$), intersection ($\cap$) and difference ($-$).

en.q: Which model accounts for time dependent change of a model?
en.explanation: A dynamic model describes how the state of a system changes with time, usually through differential or difference equations. A static model describes the system at one time or at equilibrium, with no time dependence.
notes: Not a standard class of model.
Not a standard class of model.
facts: Static model: no time; dynamic model: the state changes with time.

en.q: Which model is the one in which every set of variable states is uniquely determined by parameters in the model and by sets of previous states of these variables?
en.explanation: If the parameters and the earlier states fix every later state uniquely, there is no randomness: the model is deterministic. A probabilistic (stochastic) model gives only a distribution of possible states.
notes: Random outcomes are not uniquely determined.
Discrete or continuous refers to time or values, not to determinism.
Discrete or continuous refers to time or values, not to determinism.
facts: Deterministic: the same inputs always give the same output; stochastic: outputs have a probability distribution.

en.q: Find the limit of the function $f(x,y)=x+y-6$ at $x=1$; $y=2$?
en.explanation: $f$ is a polynomial, hence continuous, so the limit equals the value: $1+2-6=-3$.
facts: For continuous (e.g. polynomial) $f$: $\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)}f(x,y)=f(a,b)$.

en.q: If $f(x,y)=0$ then find the directional derivative at $c=(0,0)$ along the direction $u=(a,b)$?
en.explanation: $D_uf(c)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(c+tu)-f(c)}{t}=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{0-0}{t}=0$. A constant function has zero directional derivative in every direction.
facts: $D_{\hat u}f=\nabla f\cdot\hat u$; a constant has $\nabla f=\vec0$.

en.q: If $y$ is expressed in terms of a variable $x$ as $y=f(x)$, then $y$ is called what?
en.explanation: When $y$ is given directly as $y=f(x)$ it is an explicit function of $x$. If the relation is only given as $F(x,y)=0$, e.g. $x^2+y^2=1$, $y$ is an implicit function of $x$.
facts: Explicit: $y=f(x)$; implicit: $F(x,y)=0$.

en.q: The sequence given by interval $[0,1]$ is ________.
en.explanation: Read 'the sequence given by interval [0,1]' as a sequence whose terms all lie in $[0,1]$. Every term lies in $[0,1]$, so $0\le a_n\le1$ for all $n$: the sequence is bounded. It need not converge: $0,1,0,1,\dots$ has its terms in $[0,1]$ but oscillates.
notes: All the terms lie between 0 and 1.
Not necessarily: a constant sequence converges.
facts: Bounded sequence: $|a_n|\le M$ for all $n$; bounded does not imply convergent.

en.q: Suppose that $a$ is in the domain of the function $f$ such that, for all $x$ in the domain of $f$: $f(x)\le f(a)$
options: $f$ is said to have maximum value at $x=a$
$f$ is said to have minimum value at $x=a$
$f$ has both maximum and minimum values at $x=a$
en.explanation: The paper prints $f(x)<f(a)$, which fails at $x=a$ itself; it is read as $f(x)\le f(a)$. If $f(x)\le f(a)$ for every $x$ in the domain, then $f(a)$ is the greatest value of $f$: $f$ has its (absolute) maximum at $x=a$.
notes: Only a constant function has both at a point.
facts: Absolute maximum at $a$: $f(x)\le f(a)$ for all $x$ in the domain.

en.q: Which function defined on $\mathbb{R}$ by $f(x)=x$ for every $x$ in $\mathbb{R}$, is continuous in $\mathbb{R}$?
en.explanation: $f(x)=x$ is the identity function. $|f(x)-f(c)|=|x-c|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|x-c|<\delta=\varepsilon$, so it is continuous at every point.
notes: Riemann's (Thomae's) function is continuous only at the irrationals.
facts: The identity $f(x)=x$ is continuous: take $\delta=\varepsilon$.

en.q: Let $f$ and $g$ be two uniformly continuous functions on interval $I$ and also each function is bounded on $I$, then what can you say about product $f.g$?
en.explanation:
Let $|f|,|g|\le M$ on $I$. Then
$$|f(x)g(x)-f(y)g(y)|\le M\big(|g(x)-g(y)|+|f(x)-f(y)|\big),$$
which is small whenever $|x-y|$ is small, uniformly in $x,y$. So $fg$ is uniformly continuous on $I$. Boundedness is needed: $x\cdot x$ is not uniformly continuous on $\mathbb{R}$. As printed, (a) ($|fg|\le M^2$) and (d) are also true, and (c) says 'on R' where 'on I' is meant; (c) is the theorem being tested and the strongest of the three, and it is the board's key.
notes: Also true ($|fg|\le M^2$), but not the theorem being asked.
Correct (key): uniformly continuous on $I$; 'on R' should read 'on I'.
Also true (uniform continuity implies continuity), but weaker than (c).
facts: The product of two bounded uniformly continuous functions is uniformly continuous; without boundedness it can fail ($x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$).

en.q: Which condition is not required in checking for Taylor's theorem?
options: there exists a real number between $a$ and $b$
en.explanation:
Taylor's theorem needs $f^{(n-1)}$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and derivable on $(a,b)$. It then gives a number $c\in(a,b)$ with
$$f(b)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(b-a)^k+\frac{f^{(n)}(c)}{n!}(b-a)^n.$$
Boundedness of $f$ is not a hypothesis (it follows anyway from continuity on $[a,b]$). Option (c) is not a hypothesis either but the theorem's conclusion (the point $c$); the intended answer is (d), the key.
notes: Part of the statement: the point $c$.
facts: Taylor (Lagrange remainder): $f^{(n-1)}$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and derivable on $(a,b)$ ⇒ remainder $\frac{(b-a)^n}{n!}f^{(n)}(c)$.

en.q: Which of the following is not the application of Taylor's series?
options: It is used to find value of whole function
It is used in optimization techniques
It fails to solve power flow analysis
en.explanation: Taylor series let us compute a function throughout its interval of convergence from the derivatives at one point, shorten proofs and approximations, and underlie Newton-type optimisation. They are also used in power-flow (load-flow) analysis: the Newton–Raphson load-flow method linearises by a Taylor expansion. So (d) is the false claim.
notes: A genuine use: values from the derivatives at one point.
A genuine use: it simplifies proofs and limits.
A genuine use: Newton's method in optimisation.
Correct: Taylor series are used in power-flow analysis.
facts: Newton–Raphson (roots, optimisation, load flow) is a first-order Taylor expansion.

en.q: What is interval of Taylor's series expansion of $\tan(x)$?
en.explanation: $\tan x=x+\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{2x^5}{15}+\dots$ The radius of convergence is the distance from 0 to the nearest singularity, $x=\pm\frac\pi2$. So the series holds for $-\frac\pi2<x<\frac\pi2$, i.e. $(-90^\circ,90^\circ)$.
notes: Only half the interval: the series also holds for negative $x$.
$\tan x$ is infinite at $\pm\pi/2$, inside this interval.
facts: The Maclaurin series of $\tan x$ converges for $|x|<\pi/2$.

en.q: When will be matrix of derivative of $f$ given by $f(x,y)=(x-y,xy)$ will be singular?
en.explanation:
The derivative (Jacobian) matrix is
$$J=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\y&x\end{pmatrix},\qquad |J|=x+y.$$
It is singular when $x+y=0$, i.e. $x=-y$.
facts: The derivative of $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is its Jacobian matrix; singular ⇔ Jacobian determinant $=0$.

en.q: Find the simultaneous limit of function $y\sin(1/x)$?
en.explanation: The paper does not name the point; it is read as the limit as $(x,y)\to(0,0)$. There $|y\sin(1/x)|\le|y|\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\to0$, so the simultaneous (double) limit is $0$. The repeated limit $\lim_{y\to0}\lim_{x\to0}$ does not even exist, since $\sin(1/x)$ oscillates: a double limit can exist without both repeated limits.
facts: Bounded times (something tending to 0) tends to 0: $|y\sin(1/x)|\le|y|$.

en.q: While finding maximum value of a function what will we get in the case if it's second derivative becomes zero?
options: we get maxima at that point
we get minima at that point
we get both maxima and minima
en.explanation: If $f'(c)=0$ and $f''(c)=0$ the second-derivative test fails: $c$ may be a maximum ($-x^4$), a minimum ($x^4$) or a point of inflection ($x^3$), all at $0$. One must look at higher derivatives or at the sign change of $f'$: the point is only a possible inflection point.
notes: Correct: the test is inconclusive and an inflection is possible.
facts: $f''(c)=0$: the test fails; use the first non-zero higher derivative (odd order ⇒ inflection, even order ⇒ extremum).

en.q: Find curl $(\vec r)$ if $\vec r=2xy\,\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$.
en.explanation:
$$\nabla\times\vec r=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\partial_x&\partial_y&\partial_z\\2xy&1&1\end{vmatrix}=\hat k\left(0-\frac{\partial(2xy)}{\partial y}\right)=-2x\,\hat k$$
The $\hat i$ and $\hat j$ components vanish because the components are free of $z$ and the last two are constants.
notes: Differentiates $2xy$ with respect to $x$ instead of $y$.
The $\hat k$ component $-\partial_y(2xy)$ is not zero.
facts: $\hat k$-component of curl $\vec F$: $\partial_xF_2-\partial_yF_1$.

en.q: Find the double integral of $f(x,y,z)=(y+z)dx+(z+x)dy+(x+y)dz$.
en.explanation: The paper's 'double integral of f(x,y,z) = …' is garbled; it is read as the integral of this differential form round a closed curve (or, by Stokes' theorem, the flux of its curl), the only readings that give a number. The integrand is an exact differential: $(y+z)dx+(z+x)dy+(x+y)dz=d(xy+yz+zx)$; equivalently $\vec F=(y+z,\,z+x,\,x+y)$ has $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec0$. So its integral round any closed curve is $0$.
notes: Correct: an exact differential integrated round a closed path.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: If $\vec F=\nabla\phi$ (curl $\vec F=\vec0$ on a simply connected region), then $\oint_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=0$.

en.q: How do we find volume of a solid surface?
options: By triple integrating it over the surface
en.explanation: The volume of a solid region $V$ is $\iiint_V dx\,dy\,dz$, a triple integral over the region bounded by the surface. A double integral $\iint f\,dA$ gives a volume only under a surface $z=f(x,y)$, and a surface integral gives area or flux.
notes: Gives a volume only for the region under a surface $z=f(x,y)$.
Correct (strictly, over the region the surface encloses).
A line integral gives work or circulation.
A surface integral gives area or flux.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: Volume $=\iiint_V dV$; area $=\iint_R dA$.

en.q: Which theorem is valid in calculating integral for a multiple connected domain $R$?
en.explanation: Green's theorem $\oint_C(M\,dx+N\,dy)=\iint_R\left(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy$ also holds for a multiply connected plane region when $C$ is its whole boundary, the outer curve taken anticlockwise and the inner curves clockwise: cut the region into simply connected pieces and add.
notes: Relates a solid to its closed boundary surface, not a plane region.
Relates an open surface to its boundary curve.
A method of evaluation, not a theorem.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: Green's theorem extends to multiply connected regions if the holes are traversed clockwise.

en.q: The functions which are present on one side of Green's theorem are of which kind?
en.explanation: Green's theorem needs $M(x,y)$, $N(x,y)$ and the partial derivatives $\partial M/\partial y$, $\partial N/\partial x$ to be continuous on $R$ and its boundary. The double-integral side contains $\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}$.
notes: The partial derivatives must also be continuous.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: Green: $\oint_C M\,dx+N\,dy=\iint_R(N_x-M_y)\,dA$, with $M,N,M_y,N_x$ continuous.

en.q: The oscillation of a bounded function $f$ on an interval $[a,b]$ is the ________ of the set $\{|f(x)-f(y)|\}$ of the numbers.
en.explanation: The oscillation is $\omega=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:x,y\in[a,b]\}=M-m$, where $M$ and $m$ are the supremum and infimum of $f$. It is a supremum, not a maximum, because the largest difference need not be attained.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: Oscillation $=M-m=\sup|f(x)-f(y)|$.

en.q: The necessary and sufficient condition for a function $f$ to be Riemann integrable is that for every partition $P$ for every $\varepsilon>0$; which of the following condition must occur?
en.explanation: Riemann's criterion: a bounded $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ iff for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a partition $P$ with $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$; every refinement of $P$ then works too. (The paper's 'for every partition P' should read 'for some partition P'.)
notes: The gap must be made smaller than every $\varepsilon$.
The gap must be made smaller than every $\varepsilon$.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: Riemann's criterion: for every $\varepsilon>0$ some partition $P$ has $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$.

en.q: Pick the correct statement?
options: Every continuous function is Riemann integrable
Every monotonic increasing function $f$ is not Riemann integrable
Every continuous function is not Riemann integrable
If function is increasing in interval it is not increasing in each of its subinterval
en.explanation: On a closed interval $[a,b]$ a continuous function is uniformly continuous, so $U-L$ can be made as small as we like: it is Riemann integrable. Monotonic functions on $[a,b]$ are integrable too, so (b) and (c) are false; a function increasing on an interval is increasing on each subinterval, so (d) is false.
notes: Increasing on an interval ⇒ increasing on each subinterval.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: Continuous or monotonic on $[a,b]$ ⇒ Riemann integrable.

en.q: Every absolutely convergent improper integral is ________.
en.explanation: If $\int_a^\infty|f|\,dx$ converges then, by the Cauchy criterion, $\left|\int_{x_1}^{x_2}f\,dx\right|\le\int_{x_1}^{x_2}|f|\,dx\to0$, so $\int_a^\infty f\,dx$ converges. The converse fails: $\int_1^\infty\frac{\sin x}{x}dx$ converges, but not absolutely.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: Absolute convergence ⇒ convergence (for series and for improper integrals).

en.q: If $f$ is the derivative of some function on $[a,b]$, then there exists a number $c$ in $(a,b)$ such that integral of $f$ with respect to $x$ (from $a$ to $b$) $=$ ________.
en.explanation: Let $f=F'$ (and $f$ integrable). Then $\int_a^bf\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$, and Lagrange's mean value theorem gives $F(b)-F(a)=F'(c)(b-a)=f(c)(b-a)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$.
facts: Mean value theorem for integrals: $\int_a^bf\,dx=f(c)(b-a)$.

en.q: Find the limit point of the sequence $\langle1,2,\tfrac12,3,\tfrac13,\dots\rangle$
en.explanation: The odd-placed terms $1,\frac12,\frac13,\dots$ tend to $0$, so $0$ is a limit point. The even-placed terms $2,3,4,\dots$ go to $\infty$, and no other real number is approached by infinitely many terms. So $0$ is the only limit point (the sequence is unbounded, so it does not converge).
facts: A limit point of a sequence is the limit of some subsequence.

en.q: Every uniformly continuous function on an interval is ________ on that interval.
en.explanation: Uniform continuity: for every $\varepsilon>0$ one $\delta$ works for all pairs of points. Fixing one point of the pair gives ordinary continuity there, so uniform continuity implies continuity. The converse fails: $1/x$ on $(0,1)$.
notes: A term for sequences, not functions.
A term for sequences, not functions.
A term for sequences, not functions.
facts: Uniformly continuous ⇒ continuous; on $[a,b]$ the converse holds too.

en.q: If $f=\langle1/n\rangle$, then what can you say about monotonic nature of $f$?
en.explanation: The paper prints 'If =<1/n>', with $f$ missing; it is read as $f=\langle1/n\rangle$. $\frac1{n+1}<\frac1n$ for every $n$, so $f_{n+1}<f_n$: the sequence $1,\frac12,\frac13,\dots$ is (strictly) monotonically decreasing. Option (a) 'monotonic' is also true, but (c) is the precise answer (key).
notes: Only a constant sequence is both.
facts: $\langle1/n\rangle$ is strictly decreasing, bounded, and converges to 0.

en.q: The expansion of power series having $R$ as the radius of convergence and $x,a$ be any two points in $\mathbb{R}$, converges if ________.
en.explanation: A power series $\sum c_n(x-a)^n$ with radius of convergence $R$ converges (absolutely) for $|x-a|<R$ and diverges for $|x-a|>R$; at $|x-a|=R$ it may or may not converge.
notes: The end points must be tested separately.
It always converges at $x=a$, and for $|x-a|<R$.
facts: $R=\lim|c_n/c_{n+1}|$ (when it exists): convergent inside, divergent outside, test the ends.

en.q: What powers of $x$ does expansion of $\sin(x)$ contains?
en.explanation: $\sin x=x-\frac{x^3}{3!}+\frac{x^5}{5!}-\dots$: only odd powers, because $\sin x$ is an odd function. ($\cos x$, an even function, has only even powers.)
notes: Too vague: it is the odd powers.
facts: An odd function has only odd powers in its Maclaurin series; an even function only even powers.

en.q: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space then what can you say about $X$ and $d$?
options: $d$ is called metric and $X$ is called ground set
$d$ is called metric but can't say about $X$
$X$ is called metric and $d$ is called ground set
en.explanation: In $(X,d)$, $X$ is the underlying (ground) set and $d:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ is the metric (distance function): $d\ge0$, $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and the triangle inequality.
notes: $d$ is a function, not a set of points.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Metric space $(X,d)$: the set $X$ with the metric $d$.

en.q: If we are given two overlapping sets $A$ and $B$ in metric space then what can we say about $d(A,B)$?
en.explanation: $d(A,B)=\inf\{d(a,b):a\in A,\ b\in B\}$. If $A\cap B\ne\varnothing$, take $a=b$ in the overlap: $d(a,b)=0$, so $d(A,B)=0$.
notes: The infimum always exists, since distances are $\ge0$.
True but not precise: it is exactly 0.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: $d(A,B)=\inf d(a,b)$; $A\cap B\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow d(A,B)=0$ (the converse fails).

en.q: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $P_n$ be the Cauchy sequence defined then $\{P_n\}$ is ________.
en.explanation: Every Cauchy sequence is bounded: with $\varepsilon=1$, all terms beyond some $N$ lie within 1 of $P_N$, and only finitely many come before. It need not converge unless $X$ is complete: in $\mathbb{Q}$, $1,\ 1.4,\ 1.41,\ 1.414,\dots$ is Cauchy, but its limit $\sqrt2$ is not in $\mathbb{Q}$. The board's key is (a) 'convergent', which is wrong here: a Cauchy sequence converges only in a complete space, and the question says only that $(X,d)$ is a metric space. (c) merely repeats the hypothesis.
notes: The key; true only when $X$ is complete.
A Cauchy sequence never diverges to infinity.
Correct: every Cauchy sequence is bounded.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Cauchy ⇒ bounded always; Cauchy ⇒ convergent only in a complete space.

en.q: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $E$ is contained in $X$, $E$ is called nowhere dense set if ________.
options: closure of $E$ terminate after some steps
en.explanation: $E$ is nowhere dense if the interior of its closure is empty: $(\overline E)^\circ=\varnothing$. Examples: $\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{R}$, the Cantor set. The closure itself is empty only when $E=\varnothing$. The paper's option (a) leaves out 'interior of': as printed, 'closure of E is empty' would force $E=\varnothing$; it is still the intended answer (key), the other options being meaningless.
notes: The intended answer, with 'interior of' missing: $(\overline E)^\circ=\varnothing$.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Nowhere dense: $\operatorname{int}(\overline E)=\varnothing$.

en.q: Which statement states that "Every complete metric space is of second category"?
en.explanation: Baire's category theorem: a complete metric space is not a countable union of nowhere dense sets, i.e. it is of the second category (in itself).
notes: Cantor's intersection theorem is a tool in its proof, not this statement.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Baire: a complete metric space is of the second category (not a countable union of nowhere dense sets).

en.q: In metric space which function is always continuous?
en.explanation: For a fixed $y$, $|d(x,y)-d(x',y)|\le d(x,x')$ by the triangle inequality, so $x\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous (indeed 1-Lipschitz); $d$ is continuous on $X\times X$ as well.
notes: Trivially continuous by its name; not a particular function.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: $|d(x,z)-d(y,z)|\le d(x,y)$: the distance function is continuous.

en.q: If $f$ is a continuous function from $X$ to $Y$, then this property is called?
en.explanation: The stem is garbled ('then this property is called'); it is read as: what is a property called that a continuous map carries from $X$ to its image? A property of a space that passes to its image under every continuous map is called a continuous invariant: if $f:X\to Y$ is continuous and onto and $X$ has the property, so does $Y$. Compactness and connectedness are examples.
notes: Completeness is not preserved: $\tan^{-1}$ maps $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Compactness and connectedness are continuous invariants; completeness is not.

en.q: Which of the following metric space is not complete?
en.explanation: With the usual metric $\mathbb{Q}$ is not complete: $1,\ 1.4,\ 1.41,\dots$ (decimal approximations of $\sqrt2$) is Cauchy with no limit in $\mathbb{Q}$. $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ are complete. The irrationals are not complete either: $\sqrt2/n$ is Cauchy, but its limit $0$ is rational. Both (b) and (d) are correct; the board keyed (b).
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is complete iff it is closed; $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}-\mathbb{Q}$ are not closed.

en.q: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $B$ be a subset of $X$ then if $B$ is closed then $B$ is also ________.
en.explanation: As printed no option always holds: in $X=\mathbb{Q}$ the closed set $\mathbb{Q}$ is not complete. The paper has evidently left out 'complete' for $X$. If $X$ is complete, a Cauchy sequence in $B$ converges in $X$, and since $B$ is closed its limit lies in $B$: $B$ is complete. Closed sets need not be compact or bounded ($[0,\infty)$ in $\mathbb{R}$), nor unbounded ($[0,1]$).
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete; a complete subspace of any metric space is closed.

en.q: Inner automorphism corresponding to every element of an abelian group is?
en.explanation: The inner automorphism by $a$ is $T_a(x)=axa^{-1}$. In an abelian group $axa^{-1}=aa^{-1}x=x$, so every $T_a$ is the identity map: $\mathrm{Inn}(G)=\{I\}$ is trivial.
notes: Not a property of a map.
Not a property of a map.
facts: $\mathrm{Inn}(G)\cong G/Z(G)$; it is trivial iff $G$ is abelian.

en.q: A group is called abelian if it satisfies ________ property.
en.explanation: Every group is associative and has an identity and inverses. It is abelian when, in addition, $ab=ba$ for all $a,b$: the commutative property.
facts: Abelian group = group + commutativity.

en.q: Every element of a group $G$ when expressed as internal direct product of $a,b,c,\dots z$ if and only if every element is uniquely expressed as?
en.explanation: The stem is garbled; it asks for the standard criterion. $G$ is the internal direct product of its normal subgroups $A,B,\dots,Z$ iff every $g\in G$ can be written uniquely as a product $g=ab\cdots z$ with $a\in A,\ b\in B,\dots,z\in Z$. The group operation is written as multiplication.
notes: The group operation is written as a product, not a sum.
facts: $G=A\times B$ (internal) ⇔ $A,B\trianglelefteq G$, $G=AB$ and $A\cap B=\{e\}$ ⇔ each $g=ab$ uniquely (with normality).

en.q: If a group $G$ is internal direct product of its subgroups $A,B,C,\dots,Z$ then $G$ is isomorphic to ________.
en.explanation: The map $A\times B\times\dots\times Z\to G$, $(a,b,\dots,z)\mapsto ab\cdots z$, is an isomorphism: elements of different factors commute and the representation is unique. So an internal direct product is isomorphic to the external direct product of the same subgroups.
notes: That is $G$ itself; trivially true but not the theorem.
facts: Internal direct product ≅ external direct product of the same factors.

en.q: The external direct product of two cyclic groups is ________.
en.explanation: $\mathbb{Z}_m\oplus\mathbb{Z}_n$ is cyclic iff $\gcd(m,n)=1$: $\mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\mathbb{Z}_3\cong\mathbb{Z}_6$ is cyclic, but $\mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2$ (the Klein four-group) is not. So it need not be cyclic. Option (c) 'abelian' is also true (cyclic groups are abelian, and so is their direct product); the board keyed (b).
notes: Also true: cyclic groups are abelian, and so is their product.
facts: $\mathbb{Z}_m\oplus\mathbb{Z}_n$ is cyclic ⇔ $\gcd(m,n)=1$.

en.q: Name the smallest non cyclic group.
en.explanation: Groups of order 1, 2 and 3 (trivial or prime order) are cyclic. Of the two groups of order 4, $\mathbb{Z}_4$ is cyclic, while the Klein four-group $K_4=\{e,a,b,ab\}$, in which every non-identity element has order 2, is not. So $K_4$ is the smallest non-cyclic group.
notes: A group of prime order $p$ is cyclic.
facts: $K_4\cong\mathbb{Z}_2\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2$ is the smallest non-cyclic group.

en.q: What are no. of elements of order 100 of $\mathbb{Z}_{200}$?
en.explanation: In a cyclic group of order $n$, for each divisor $d$ of $n$ there are exactly $\phi(d)$ elements of order $d$. Since $100\mid200$, the number is $\phi(100)=100\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac45=40$.
notes: That is $\phi(200)$, the number of generators.
facts: Cyclic group of order $n$: $\phi(d)$ elements of order $d$ for each $d\mid n$.

notes: Not this product: 1 must go to 5.
path: 4.4 Permutations and the symmetric group Sn
facts: Multiply permutations right to left: follow each symbol through the right-hand factor first.

en.q: Let $k$ be the number of the $p$-ssg of a finite group $G$. Then ________.
en.explanation: ('$p$-ssg' = Sylow $p$-subgroup.) By Sylow's theorems the number $n_p$ of Sylow $p$-subgroups equals the index $[G:N(P)]$ of the normaliser of one of them, so it divides $o(G)$; moreover $n_p\equiv1\pmod p$. Example: $S_4$ has $n_3=4$, and $4\mid24$.
notes: Sylow $p$-subgroups always exist (if $p\nmid o(G)$, $k=1$: the trivial subgroup).
facts: Sylow: $n_p\equiv1\pmod p$ and $n_p\mid o(G)/p^a$.

en.q: If $f(z)$ is analytic function whose real part is constant then $f(z)$ is ________.
en.explanation: Let $f=u+iv$ with $u=c$. Then $u_x=u_y=0$, and the Cauchy–Riemann equations $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ give $v_x=v_y=0$, so $v$ is constant too. Hence $f'(z)=u_x+iv_x=0$ and $f$ is constant (on a domain).
facts: Analytic with constant real part, imaginary part or modulus ⇒ constant.

en.q: Does C-R equations are necessary and sufficient for a function to be analytic?
options: can't say about nature of equations
en.explanation: The Cauchy–Riemann equations are necessary but not sufficient. $f(z)=\sqrt{|xy|}$ satisfies them at $0$ (all four partial derivatives are 0 there) but is not differentiable at $0$: along $y=x$ the difference quotient tends to $\pm\frac{1}{1+i}$, not 0. They become sufficient when the partial derivatives are also continuous.
facts: C–R equations + continuous first partial derivatives ⇒ analytic.

en.q: Which theorem states that "An integral function attains every finite value with atmost one possible exception"?
en.explanation: Picard's (little) theorem: a non-constant entire (integral) function takes every finite complex value with at most one exception; $e^z$ omits only $0$.
notes: Relates the zeros of $f$ to $\log|f|$ on a circle.
Says $|f(z)|\le|z|$ for analytic $f$ mapping the unit disc into itself with $f(0)=0$.
facts: Picard: a non-constant entire function omits at most one value ($e^z$ omits 0).
